item.title: “When, monks, a monk is not lustful regarding objects that can provoke lust, and his self is free from lust; is not hateful regarding objects…
item.description:
“When, monks, a monk is not lustful regarding objects that can provoke lust, and his self is free from lust; is not hateful regarding objects that can provoke hatred, and his self is free from hatred; is not deluded regarding objects that can provoke delusion, and his self is free from delusion; is not infatuated regarding objects that can provoke infatuation, and his self is free from infatuation — then he has no fear, no trembling, no terror, does not fall into fear, and does not go by whatever ascetics may say.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.117

item.title: “For a person who lives heedlessly, Craving grows like a creeping vine. He leaps from life to life, Like a monkey seeking fruit in the…
item.description:
“For a person who lives heedlessly,
Craving grows like a creeping vine.
He leaps from life to life,
Like a monkey seeking fruit in the forest.”

“Whoever in this world is overcome by this wretched clinging,
His sorrows increase like well-watered birana grass.”

“Whoever in this world overcomes this wretched clinging,
Sorrows fall away from him like water drops from a lotus.”

From: Dhammapada 334-359

item.title: “Poṭṭhapāda, I teach the Dhamma for the removal of gross personality view. If you practice accordingly, then defiling states are abandoned, pure states increase, and…
item.description:
“Poṭṭhapāda, I teach the Dhamma for the removal of gross personality view. If you practice accordingly, then defiling states are abandoned, pure states increase, and in this very life, by direct knowledge, you realize and abide in full, vast wisdom. Poṭṭhapāda, you might think: ‘Defiling states will be abandoned, pure states will increase, and in this very life, by direct knowledge, one realizes and abides in full, vast wisdom — yet suffering still remains.’ Poṭṭhapāda, do not think thus. When defiling states are abandoned, pure states increase, and in this very life, by direct knowledge, one realizes and abides in full, vast wisdom — then gladness arises, joy, tranquility, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and a pleasant abiding arise.”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 9 – Poṭṭhapādasutta

item.title: “Pleasant and delightful are sensual pleasures, In various forms both coarse and refined — Seeing the danger in these strands of pleasure, Wander alone like…
item.description:
“Pleasant and delightful are sensual pleasures,
In various forms both coarse and refined —
Seeing the danger in these strands of pleasure,
Wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.”

“This is a boil, this is a calamity,
This is a disease, this is a dart —
Seeing the danger in these strands of pleasure,
Wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.”

From: Sutta Nipāta 1.3

item.title: “Truly, brahmins, this world is led by aging, illness, and death. Since the world is led by aging, illness, and death, brahmins, restraint of body,…
item.description:
“Truly, brahmins, this world is led by aging, illness, and death. Since the world is led by aging, illness, and death, brahmins, restraint of body, speech, and mind in this life is a refuge, a cave, an island (or a lamp), a shelter, and a destination for one who has gone to death.

When a house is on fire,
The goods that are removed
Are useful to the owners,
Not those burned inside.
So too, the world is burning
With aging and death on fire —
Save yourself by giving,
For what is given is well-saved.
Here, restraint of body,
Restraint of speech and mind —
One who does this, even while dying,
Experiences happiness,
Because while still alive,
He has made merit.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.52
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “That is so, great king. Few are those in the world who, having obtained abundant, great wealth, do not become infatuated, do not become intoxicated,…
item.description:
“That is so, great king. Few are those in the world who, having obtained abundant, great wealth, do not become infatuated, do not become intoxicated, do not fall into heedlessness regarding sensual pleasures, and do not act wrongly toward others. But many are those in the world who, having obtained abundant, great wealth, become infatuated, intoxicated, fall into heedlessness regarding sensual pleasures, and act wrongly toward others.

Bemused by wealth and sensual pleasures,
People are greedy and deluded,
In the midst of sensual pleasures,
Without clear awareness,
They are overly intoxicated,
Like a deer unaware of the trap set —
Later they suffer,
Experiencing the results of evil deeds.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.6

item.title: Behold this decorated image — A heap of wounds, a collection of sores, Diseased, the object of many lustful thoughts, Nothing stable or permanent here.…
item.description:
Behold this decorated image —
A heap of wounds, a collection of sores,
Diseased, the object of many lustful thoughts,
Nothing stable or permanent here.

Behold this adorned appearance,
With jewels and earrings,
A skeleton covered by skin,
Made beautiful by clothes.

The feet are painted with lac and dye,
The face is smeared with powder and paste —
Enough to fool a fool,
But not one who seeks the far shore.

The hair is curled in seven rings,
The eyes are rubbed with collyrium and rouge —
Enough to fool a fool,
But not one who seeks the far shore.

Like a newly decorated medicine box,
This foul body is adorned for the occasion —
Enough to fool a fool,
But not one who seeks the far shore.

The hunter set his trap and snare,
The wise deer does not approach,
Having eaten the crops, we go our way,
Leaving the trapper to lament.

From: Majjhima Nikāya 82 – Raṭṭhapālasutta

item.title: “Monks, whatever is not yours, abandon it. Abandoning it will lead to your happiness and well-being. And what, monks, is not yours? The eye, monks,…
item.description:
“Monks, whatever is not yours, abandon it. Abandoning it will lead to your happiness and well-being. And what, monks, is not yours? The eye, monks, is not yours — abandon it. Abandoning it will lead to your happiness and well-being. Forms are not yours — abandon them. Eye-consciousness is not yours — abandon it. Eye-contact is not yours — abandon it. Suppose, monks, a person were to carry away, burn, or do whatever they want with all the grass, sticks, branches, and leaves in this Jeta’s Grove. Would you think: ‘This person carries us away, burns us, or does whatever they want with us’?” - “No, venerable sir.” - “Why not?” - “Because that is not our self nor belonging to our self.” - “So too, monks, the eye is not yours — abandon it … Forms … Eye-consciousness … Eye-contact … Whatever feeling arises dependent on mind-contact — pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant — that feeling is not yours. Abandon it. Abandoning it will lead to your happiness and well-being.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.101

item.title: “And what, monks, is the origin of suffering? Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact…
item.description:
“And what, monks, is the origin of suffering? Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling. With feeling as condition, craving. This is the origin of suffering. Dependent on the ear … on the nose … on the tongue … on the body … Dependent on the mind and phenomena, mind-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling. With feeling as condition, craving. This, monks, is the origin of suffering.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.106
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “And how, monks, is there restraint? Here, monks, when a monk sees a form with the eye, he is not attached to agreeable forms nor…
item.description:
“And how, monks, is there restraint? Here, monks, when a monk sees a form with the eye, he is not attached to agreeable forms nor repelled by disagreeable forms. He dwells with bodily mindfulness established, with an immeasurable mind. He knows as it actually is the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. Here, evil, unwholesome states that have arisen are abandoned without remainder. When he tastes a flavor … When he cognizes a phenomenon with the mind, he is not attached to agreeable phenomena nor repelled by disagreeable phenomena. He dwells with bodily mindfulness established, with an immeasurable mind. He knows as it actually is the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. Here, evil, unwholesome states that have arisen are abandoned without remainder. Thus, monks, is restraint.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.244
